items.title: How Close Is Recursive Self-Improvement? A Review of the Evidence – Forecasting Research Institute
items.content: Published: Nov 24, 2026 Share View PDF X (Twitter) LinkedIn mail Copy URL Working paper Working paper How Close Is Recursive Self-Improvement? A Review of the Evidence How Close Is Recursive Self-Improvement? A Review of the Evidence We review the evidence, existing forecasts, and key disagreements, turn the disagreements into forecasting questions, and give automated forecasts from an ensemble of frontier LLMs. Simas Kučinskas, Nick Merrill, and Josh Rosenberg Published: Nov 24, 2026 Share View PDF X (Twitter) LinkedIn mail Copy URL Contents Simas Kučinskas, Nick Merrill, and Josh Rosenberg Summary AI companies increasingly state that their models may soon be capable of recursive self-improvement (RSI), which could dramatically accelerate AI capability progress. How close is RSI? We review the evidence, existing forecasts, and key disagreements, turn the disagreements into forecasting questions, and provide forecasts from an ensemble of frontier large language models (LLMs) in an automated dashboard. As of Nov 2026, AI acts as a highly capable research assistant, but humans still supply most of the research judgment. AI capability progress has not clearly accelerated on public measures, but there is internal evidence from AI companies indicating acceleration. On a simple extrapolation of current trends, mostly using company-reported metrics, AI could take over most AI R&D tasks by 2027–2028, in line with OpenAI’s target of an automated AI researcher by Mar 2028. A key uncertainty is whether these trends continue as the remaining non-automated tasks increasingly require research judgment. To measure acceleration, we propose a forecasting question on the likelihood of a fast year : any 12 months in which the frontier of the Epoch Capabilities Index rises by 30 points or more, about twice its pace since Sep 2024. We provide an automated dashboard with forecasts from an ensemble of frontier LLMs. As of Nov 20, 2026, the LLM ensemble forecasts about a 36% chance of a fast year by the end of 2027 and about a 61% chance by the end of 2030. If a fast year happens, the ensemble gives about a 76% chance that AI automation of AI R&D caused it. DATA CUTOFF: NOV 20, 2026 View the automated dashboard Acknowledgements We thank Sivan Livnat for research assistance. For feedback and input at various stages of the project, we thank Jason Abaluck, Zack Devlin-Foltz, Basil Halperin, Ezra Karger, Matt Reynolds, Luis Enrique Urtubey De Cesaris, and Bridget Williams. Changelog Key changes in v2: Added METR’s Nov 2026 assessment of AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic ( Section 3.1.2 ). Both AI companies now report that they have crossed their own AI R&D thresholds ( Sections 2.1 and 4.1 ). Added evidence on harder-to-verify tasks from METR and Epoch ( Section 3.2 ), and METR’s updated time horizons ( Sections 3.1 and 4.3.3 ). Updated the trend extrapolations from Peter Wildeford’s dashboard, the prediction-market forecasts, and the individual forecasts, several of which changed after METR’s Nov 5 report ( Section 4 ). Updated the evidence from AI companies and public benchmarks ( Sections 3.1 and 3.2 ), and switched to Epoch AI’s new Bayesian ECI ( Section 2.3 ). Revised the crux framework so that Step 1 asks whether AI greatly speeds up AI R&D, because acceleration does not need full automation ( Section 5 ). Replaced the one-time LLM forecasts (Oct 29, 2026) with an automated weekly dashboard ( Section 6.1 ). Updated our plans for human forecasts: we will ask some of the questions in an upcoming LEAP wave ( Sections 1 and 6 ). Moved the estimate of the internal lead to a new Appendix A , now based on METR’s data. Previous versions (PDF) v1 1. Introduction How quickly will AI improve between now and 2030? There are three broad possibilities: AI progress could slow down, continue at its current pace, or accelerate. A particularly important scenario is acceleration driven by AI systems that help build future AI systems . The International AI Safety Report 2026 (IASR) notes that “ positive feedback loops – such as AI systems contributing to AI research – could accelerate progress ” and “ decades of progress could happen in years ” ( IASR , §1.3). This positive feedback loop is often called recursive self-improvement (RSI) ( Yudkowsky, 2008 ): AI systems automate AI R&D and build better successor systems in a recursive loop (see Figure 1). Figure 1: The RSI loop, in which each generation of AI systems helps develop the next. RSI could bring about large benefits as well as substantial risks. A Sep 2026 report by AI researchers including Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, and Anthropic cofounder Jack Clark argues that RSI could bring AI’s benefits forward by years. However, RSI could also pose extreme risks, as humanity may fail to keep up with the growth in capabilities or lose oversight of advanced AI systems ( Chan et al., 2026 ). Recent reports review RSI with a focus on its risks and on policy res

items.title: The Guardian view on AI and the Riemann hypothesis: a triumph of intelligence, a test of democracy | Editorial
items.content: Machines are solving problems that have been beyond the reach of human ingenuity. Their growing power must not become the sole preserve of billionairesFor the average person, the news that AI has helped crack a problem that has defied mathematicians since 1859 might elicit momentary awe. What ought to worry everyone is not the discovery per se, but what it says about the power of the machines making it. The pace of scientific discovery looks like it is outrunning the ability of humanity – and its institutions – to understand, let alone regulate, AI’s advances.Last Friday Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said that he, with the assistance of an unreleased version of the company’s Claude chatbot, had produced what many mathematicians see as the holy grail: a proof for the Riemann hypothesis. Mathematicians like Cornell University’s Steven Strogatz had already cried on podcasts, lamenting that students were asking: “What’s the point if the AI can do math better than any human being?” Computers can validate the Alpöge-Claude proof. But Prof Strogatz fears AI’s discoveries may soon defy human understanding. Asking AI to explain them, he said, would be like him trying to teach calculus to his own dog.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? items.title: This ER Doctor Became a Hospital’s First Clinical AI Engineer
items.content: When Boston Children’s Hospital posted a job listing for a prompt engineer in 2023, Dinesh Rai decided to apply. He didn’t expect to get the job.At the time, prompt engineering was being touted as one of the hot new jobs created by generative AI. Companies wanted people who knew how to coax the best answers from large language models (LLMs) by carefully wording instructions, supplying examples, and giving the systems personas or other context.Dinesh RaiEmployer: Boston Children’s HospitalOccupation: Clinical AI EngineerEducation: Bachelor’s degree in supply-chain management and marketing sciences, Rutgers Business School; Doctor of Medicine, Albert Einstein College of MedicineIt was an unusual role for a hospital, but Rai had an unusual résumé. While he was trained as an emergency physician, he had also taught himself to code just before entering medical school. After completing a fellowship in clinical informatics—which focuses on the intersection of clinical practice and IT systems—he moved into health technology. Boston Children’s brought him on board in August 2023. Three years later, Rai still works there. Prompt engineering, however, has become a much less important part of the job.When he joined, the expectation was that prompting would become a job in itself. “Knowing how to prompt AI properly was going to be the job function of the future,” says John Brownstein, chief innovation officer at Boston Children’s.Early on, the hospital needed internal expertise about how to begin using AI, Brownstein says. Now, better models have made elaborate prompting less important, so the harder work is building AI into actual health care systems—and determining whether its answers can be trusted. Brownstein says the questions they focus on these days have shifted: “How do you embed these tools in your day-to-day operations? How do you build agents to manage literally everything that you do?”For Rai, that has meant embracing a job broader than the role that brought him to Boston. “I’m more like a clinical AI engineer now,” he says.Between medicine and engineeringRai originally studied business as an undergraduate and began teaching himself to code in 2014 (the same year he entered medical school), as neural networks and image recognition were starting to attract wider attention. He kept building software while training as a doctor. In medical school, for instance, he created a platform called Academius for students to track residency interviews and assemble their rank lists.For Rai, the appeal of coding was its scale. In emergency medicine, he could make a direct difference for the individual patient in front of him. Software offered the possibility of building something that thousands of clinicians might use for many more patients.His 2021–22 informatics fellowship made the possibility of doing that full-time feel real. In 2022, Rai took a job at Pieces, a health care AI company, where he led work to bring LLM-based medical summarization into clinical use.That meant taking a break from practicing medicine altogether. “Stepping away was definitely a hard decision,” Rai says. But he wanted to give the technology work his full attention. He has since reactivated his medical license and hopes to return to clinical practice in some capacity within the next year.At Boston Children’s, roughly half his day now looks like an engineer’s: working with developers, writing code, and advancing projects from the technical side. The other half is spent with clinicians, figuring out what they actually need. That combination has become the point of the job. Uncovering “clinical doppelgangers”One project, called clinical doppelgangers, is designed to help doctors treating complicated patients find similar cases buried in the hospital’s historical data. Medical guidelines are generally based on large populations, but at a hospital that handles rare and complex diseases, an individual child may not fit neatly into the populations represented in published studies.The system is being developed to let clinicians identify previous patients with relevant similarities, examine their trajectories, and see how different interventions turned out. It is not meant to replace randomized clinical trials. Instead, it could provide another source of evidence when a physician is facing a case for which the published literature offers little guidance.Projects like that require more than knowing how to ask an LLM the right question. They require understanding what hospital data means, how a clinician will use an answer, and how an AI system can go wrong.Rai recently encountered some of those challenges while working on another project with a clinical team and a development team. They were deciding how much of a patient’s medical record to give an AI model when asking it to identify findings relevant to a particular clinical outcome.Better models have made elaborate prompting less important, so the harder work is building AI into actual health care systems.Both groups initially favored giving the model access to more information, but for different reasons. The developers assumed any data point could be useful. The clinicians assumed the model would recognize irrelevant findings and ignore them.Rai saw a problem with both assumptions. Clinically, an abnormal lab result or vital sign is not necessarily relevant to the question being asked. And from a technical perspective, an LLM cannot be counted on to recognize that irrelevance. If the system asks the model whether a given abnormality matters, it may construct a plausible explanation for why it does, even when the record does not support the connection.“That’s where the dual perspective has been valuable,” Rai says, “not just translating between teams, but recognizing when an approach that looks reasonable from either perspective rests on assumptions we shouldn’t make.”After the promptIn medicine, the challenges surrounding the prompt are now more important than polishing the prompt itself. Is the model’s output consistent with the underlying data? How should its results be evaluated? Will the clinician using it be able to recognize a mistake?That also means listening to clinicians’ experience. For the platform Rai’s team built to draft clinical notes, the clinicians who would go on to use the tool reviewed a batch of generated notes before anything was finalized. Someone who had cared for a complicated patient in the cardiac intensive care unit for weeks would catch an error far more easily than someone skimming the chart afterward, Rai says.Although AI adoption in medicine is surging, some health care professionals still have concerns about its use. “I think some skepticism is healthy, and we don’t try to talk people out of it,” he says. The team told clinicians up front that it was a generative AI tool meant to support their judgment, not replace their own review of the chart. “People trust it more when they’ve seen its mistakes than when we just tell them it’s good.”An evolving careerThe evolution of Rai’s role reflects how quickly AI-focused jobs can change, so Rai is wary of telling people interested in careers like his to master any particular tool. For people who want hands-on engineering jobs, fundamental programming skills still matter. Some understanding of machine learning is useful, as is experience building and testing systems. But not every clinician who wants to work with AI needs to become a database architect or take a deep dive into algorithms.What Rai considers indispensable is domain knowledge. In the medical field, that means understanding how health care workflows operate, how electronic health record data is created, what that data actually represents, and where care breaks down.That may be the more durable lesson from a career that briefly carried one of AI’s buzziest job titles. “The value isn’t just knowing how to get an answer from a model,” Rai says. “It’s knowing what context it needs and whether that context supports the answer we’re asking it to give.”

items.content_html: When Boston Children’s Hospital posted a job listing for a prompt engineer in 2023, Dinesh Rai decided to apply. He didn’t expect to get the job.At the time, prompt engineering was being touted as one of the hot new jobs created by generative AI. Companies wanted people who knew how to coax the best answers from large language models (LLMs) by carefully wording instructions, supplying examples, and giving the systems personas or other context.Dinesh RaiEmployer: Boston Children’s HospitalOccupation: Clinical AI EngineerEducation: Bachelor’s degree in supply-chain management and marketing sciences, Rutgers Business School; Doctor of Medicine, Albert Einstein College of MedicineIt was an unusual role for a hospital, but Rai had an unusual résumé. While he was trained as an emergency physician, he had also taught himself to code just before entering medical school. After completing a fellowship in clinical informatics—which focuses on the intersection of clinical practice and IT systems—he moved into health technology. Boston Children’s brought him on board in August 2023. Three years later, Rai still works there. Prompt engineering, however, has become a much less important part of the job.When he joined, the expectation was that prompting would become a job in itself. “Knowing how to prompt AI properly was going to be the job function of the future,” says John Brownstein, chief innovation officer at Boston Children’s.Early on, the hospital needed internal expertise about how to begin using AI, Brownstein says. Now, better models have made elaborate prompting less important, so the harder work is building AI into actual health care systems—and determining whether its answers can be trusted. Brownstein says the questions they focus on these days have shifted: “How do you embed these tools in your day-to-day operations? How do you build agents to manage literally everything that you do?”For Rai, that has meant embracing a job broader than the role that brought him to Boston. “I’m more like a clinical AI engineer now,” he says.Between medicine and engineeringRai originally studied business as an undergraduate and began teaching himself to code in 2014 (the same year he entered medical school), as neural networks and image recognition were starting to attract wider attention. He kept building software while training as a doctor. In medical school, for instance, he created a platform called Academius for students to track residency interviews and assemble their rank lists.For Rai, the appeal of coding was its scale. In emergency medicine, he could make a direct difference for the individual patient in front of him. Software offered the possibility of building something that thousands of clinicians might use for many more patients.His 2021–22 informatics fellowship made the possibility of doing that full-time feel real. In 2022, Rai took a job at Pieces, a health care AI company, where he led work to bring LLM-based medical summarization into clinical use.That meant taking a break from practicing medicine altogether. “Stepping away was definitely a hard decision,” Rai says. But he wanted to give the technology work his full attention. He has since reactivated his medical license and hopes to return to clinical practice in some capacity within the next year.At Boston Children’s, roughly half his day now looks like an engineer’s: working with developers, writing code, and advancing projects from the technical side. The other half is spent with clinicians, figuring out what they actually need. That combination has become the point of the job. Uncovering “clinical doppelgangers”One project, called clinical doppelgangers, is designed to help doctors treating complicated patients find similar cases buried in the hospital’s historical data. Medical guidelines are generally based on large populations, but at a hospital that handles rare and complex diseases, an individual child may not fit neatly into the populations represented in published studies.The system is being developed to let clinicians identify previous patients with relevant similarities, examine their trajectories, and see how different interventions turned out. It is not meant to replace randomized clinical trials. Instead, it could provide another source of evidence when a physician is facing a case for which the published literature offers little guidance.Projects like that require more than knowing how to ask an LLM the right question. They require understanding what hospital data means, how a clinician will use an answer, and how an AI system can go wrong.Rai recently encountered some of those challenges while working on another project with a clinical team and a development team. They were deciding how much of a patient’s medical record to give an AI model when asking it to identify findings relevant to a particular clinical outcome.Better models have made elaborate prompting less important, so the harder work is building AI into actual health care systems.Both groups initially favored giving the model access to more information, but for different reasons. The developers assumed any data point could be useful. The clinicians assumed the model would recognize irrelevant findings and ignore them.Rai saw a problem with both assumptions. Clinically, an abnormal lab result or vital sign is not necessarily relevant to the question being asked. And from a technical perspective, an LLM cannot be counted on to recognize that irrelevance. If the system asks the model whether a given abnormality matters, it may construct a plausible explanation for why it does, even when the record does not support the connection.“That’s where the dual perspective has been valuable,” Rai says, “not just translating between teams, but recognizing when an approach that looks reasonable from either perspective rests on assumptions we shouldn’t make.”After the promptIn medicine, the challenges surrounding the prompt are now more important than polishing the prompt itself. Is the model’s output consistent with the underlying data? How should its results be evaluated? Will the clinician using it be able to recognize a mistake?That also means listening to clinicians’ experience. For the platform Rai’s team built to draft clinical notes, the clinicians who would go on to use the tool reviewed a batch of generated notes before anything was finalized. Someone who had cared for a complicated patient in the cardiac intensive care unit for weeks would catch an error far more easily than someone skimming the chart afterward, Rai says.Although AI adoption in medicine is surging, some health care professionals still have concerns about its use. “I think some skepticism is healthy, and we don’t try to talk people out of it,” he says. The team told clinicians up front that it was a generative AI tool meant to support their judgment, not replace their own review of the chart. “People trust it more when they’ve seen its mistakes than when we just tell them it’s good.”An evolving careerThe evolution of Rai’s role reflects how quickly AI-focused jobs can change, so Rai is wary of telling people interested in careers like his to master any particular tool. For people who want hands-on engineering jobs, fundamental programming skills still matter. Some understanding of machine learning is useful, as is experience building and testing systems. But not every clinician who wants to work with AI needs to become a database architect or take a deep dive into algorithms.What Rai considers indispensable is domain knowledge. In the medical field, that means understanding how health care workflows operate, how electronic health record data is created, what that data actually represents, and where care breaks down.That may be the more durable lesson from a career that briefly carried one of AI’s buzziest job titles. “The value isn’t just knowing how to get an answer from a model,” Rai says. “It’s knowing what context it needs and whether that context supports the answer we’re asking it to give.”

items.content_html:
Tencent has open-sourced DFly2, a speculative decoding drafter built for natively sparse LLMs. DFly2 speculative decoding targets models like DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash and Tencent’s own Hy4 flash. Its main approach is that the drafter keeps no KV cache of its own. This is important for long-context and agentic serving, where draft memory competes with concurrency.

TL;DR

Size: 0.85B-parameter, 5-layer drafter shipped with Hy4 flash.

Runs on: Serving tests used NVIDIA H20 GPUs with vLLM, TP8 per instance. Hy4 flash’s vLLM recipe defaults to 8x H200.

Performance: Higher draft acceptance than same-recipe DFlash and DSpark on all 3 targets and all general benchmarks.

Best: Up to 81% more throughput on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (SWE 64K), at matched per-user speed.

Worst: Smallest gain on Hy4 flash general tasks: only 3.9% over DSpark at temperature 0.

What is DFly2?

DFly2 is a block-parallel speculative decoding drafter from Tencent’s Hunyuan AI Infra team. It is described in the research paper ‘DFly2: Turbocharging Long-Context Speculative Decoding by Sharing the Target’s Sparsity‘.

Speculative decoding uses a small drafter to propose tokens. The target verifies them in 1 pass, so output stays lossless. Long context makes this costly. A normal drafter attends over the whole prefix and stores its own KV cache.

How does DFly2 work?

DFly2 pairs each draft layer with one sparse attention layer in the target. It shares 2 things with that layer.

KV sharing: the draft layer reads the paired target layer’s latent KV cache.

Index sharing: it attends only to positions the target’s indexer already selected (top-k sparse KV).

Initialization: each draft layer starts from its paired target layer’s weights.

Hidden injection: the target’s last-layer hidden state is gated into the draft block.

Intra-block correction: the drafter rereads the shared context slot by slot within a block.

On DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, a selection made 1 step early covers close to 90% of what later block tokens select. A same-size sliding window recovers less than 20%.

Per the AngelSpec GitHub page, each draft token attends to at most about 2K keys. So drafting cost stays roughly flat at any context length. DFly2 also skips prefill entirely. The prefill-to-decode transfer adds only 1 last-layer hidden state.

How much memory does a separate draft cache cost?

A conventional 3-layer drafter cache would add this much per token (bf16, paper Table 2):

TargetTarget KVDrafter cacheIncreaseDeepSeek-V4.1-Flash4.4 KiB3.4 KiB1.76xGLM-5.3-Flash11.7 KiB3.0 KiB1.26xHy4 flash17.2 KiB3.4 KiB1.20x

At 32K, removing the drafter’s cache lets the same memory pool hold 1.73x as many requests.

How do you deploy DFly2?

DFly2 ships inside tencent/Hy4-flash, a 220B-total, roughly 12B-active MoE with 1M context. vLLM serves it with the dfly speculative method via vllm/vllm-openai:hy4-flash. SGLang uses the DFLY algorithm via lmsysorg/sglang:hy4-flash. In the vLLM recipe, DFly speculative decoding is on by default.

items.title: AI takes a swing at physics' biggest puzzle
items.content: Home Posts AI takes a swing at physics' biggest puzzle AI takes a swing at physics' biggest puzzle PLUS: Give jobs to Nod, the personal agent from n8n Nov 27, 2026 Zach Mink , Rowan Cheung , Shubham Sharma & Jennifer Mossalgue Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 5,002 new readers. The past few months have been all about AI cracking decades-old math problems. Now it’s taking on a physics puzzle unsolved for nearly a century. Stanford physicist Venkatesa Chandrasekaran just proposed a quantum theory of gravity, developed with help from GPT-6 Astra, that could tie together the physics of planets and particles. Some physicists, however, don’t seem impressed. In today’s AI rundown: OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra helps tackle quantum gravity Rowan’s Corner: The simplest tip to improve AI output Give jobs to Nod, the personal agent from n8n Report: U.S. crackdown slows China’s AI progress LATEST DEVELOPMENTS AI IN PHYSICS ⚛️ OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra helps tackle quantum gravity Image source: Images 2.5 / The Rundown The Rundown: Stanford and OpenAI physicist Venkatesa Chandrasekaran just released an 83-page paper proposing a way to describe gravity with quantum mechanics, saying GPT-6 Astra helped develop several of its calculations and proofs over months and ~400M tokens. The details: The preprint uses the paths that light takes through spacetime to describe gravity at the quantum level, though it only covers empty space and leaves out matter. It claims to avoid the infinities that break standard gravity math, while still agreeing with known results on black holes and Einstein’s general relativity. Sam Altman praised Chandrasekaran for the work and his “confidence and courage to keep pushing on something that others don’t think is possible.” Some physicists pushed back, with UCL’s Jonathan Oppenheim saying AI flagged over a dozen issues and Columbia’s Peter Woit dismissing it as a publicity stunt. items.title: SGLang on Intel Xeon CPUs and Intel GPUs as First-Class Platforms: Execution Paths and Low-Precision Inference - LMSYS Org
items.content: On this page A Shared Serving Interface, Specialized Execution Paths Intel Xeon: CPU-Native Inference Intel GPUs: Building a Native XPU Serving Stack Low-Precision MoE: A Closer Look at MXFP4 Exploring Heterogeneous Inference with EPD Co-Engineering the Future of Open AI Infrastructure What's Next Get Started on Intel Platforms Efficient LLM inference on Intel Xeon CPUs and Intel GPUs depends on optimizations tailored to each architecture. This post examines RadixArk and Intel’s collaborative work on Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (Intel AMX)-enabled computation, thread placement, and compiled execution on Intel Xeon, alongside attention and MoE kernels and graph execution on Intel GPUs. In particular, we take a closer look at the Xe2 MXFP4 path, which keeps expert weights compressed in device memory and converts weight tiles inside the compute kernel. We also describe the supported configurations and limitations of these paths. A Shared Serving Interface, Specialized Execution Paths SGLang provides a common serving interface, while each backend specializes the execution and compute paths underneath. As shown below, compute kernels implement operations such as attention and expert GEMM; the execution layer organizes the threads, buffers, and data placement needed to run them. Their interaction matters: kernel efficiency depends on the shapes, layouts, and memory access patterns produced by the surrounding execution path. Figure 1. Shared serving interface, hardware-specific execution. Support is validated per backend and configuration; the diagram does not imply feature parity or automatic CPU-GPU workload placement. Intel’s upstream work in SGLang started with CPU enablement and has progressively expanded across both Intel CPU and Intel GPU (XPU) backends, covering optimized kernels, attention and MoE, quantization, graph execution, distributed inference, model enablement, alongside continuous integration to validate changes on Intel hardware. Together, these efforts address both the performance-critical execution paths and the integration work needed to maintain backend support as SGLang evolves. On Intel Xeon, this means combining Intel AMX-enabled compute with thread placement and NUMA locality. On Intel GPUs, device dispatch and buffer organization support SYCL kernels, including grouped MoE GEMM. Both paths must preserve tensor and model semantics at the framework boundary, with correctness checked through operator tests and model-level validation. The following sections examine these CPU and GPU execution paths in more detail. Intel Xeon: CPU-Native Inference SGLang’s Xeon path combines matrix-compute acceleration with CPU-specific execution controls. The optimizations address both the arithmetic inside operators and the topology and runtime overhead around them: Intel AMX-enabled matrix compute. On supported Xeon processors, Intel AMX accelerates matrix operations in the CPU backend. This matters for dense projections and expert computation, although the benefit depends on matrix shape and batch size. W8A8 INT8 inference. The CPU path supports compatible checkpoints with 8-bit weights and activations, selected through --quantization w8a8_int8 . This reduces operand storage relative to BF16; quantization scales and model compatibility remain part of the execution contract. NUMA-aware execution and memory locality. SGLang groups physical cores using NUMA or L3-cache topology, including Xeon sub-NUMA clusters where exposed. SGLANG_CPU_OMP_THREADS_BIND provides explicit per-rank affinity control. Aligning core assignment with memory locality helps limit remote-memory traffic; adding tensor-parallel ranks also introduces communication costs. Compiled CPU execution. On Intel AMX systems, --enable-torch-compile enables CPU graph execution to reduce Python overhead. Decode uses batch-size buckets; optional prefill graphs use total-token buckets. The full prefill backend remains experimental and requires explicit enablement. These controls should be tuned together against the model, context length, and concurrency. Faster matrix kernels alone do not eliminate KV-cache traffic, NUMA effects, or parallel communication overhead. Intel GPUs: Building a Native XPU Serving Stack Intel GPU support in SGLang has followed a similar progression, moving from PyTorch XPU device enablement toward a broader optimized serving backend. SGLang’s Intel GPU backend combines SYCL kernels with serving-level execution optimizations through PyTorch’s XPU path. The work spans attention, expert computation, low precision, and generation overhead: Optimized attention kernels. The XPU kernel library includes Flash Attention and Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) implementations, with dedicated prefill and decode paths. These paths address different query sizes and KV-cache access patterns rather than treating all attention workloads as the same computation. MoE acceleration. items.content:
OCRia-1 Technical report · Blog post · Inference blog · LlamaParse · ParseBench · Ollama · GGUF OCRia-1 is a 4B vision-language model for document parsing from LlamaIndex . It reads a page
image and writes the page as Markdown, with tables in HTML, and it is built for the content that document parsers get
wrong most often: merged cells and spanning headers, tables with thousands of cells, charts whose data has to be read
off the plot, and formatting that carries meaning, such as strikethrough, underline, sub- and superscripts and
checkboxes. Accuracy: the highest-scoring open-weight model on both ParseBench leaderboards, with
visual grounding included: 85.2 on ParseBench 2 (six dimensions, seventh of 61 systems) and 84.7 on ParseBench 1
(five dimensions, second of 158). It is also first on olmOCR-bench tables and formulas, PulseBench-Tab and
fr-bench-pdf2md. See Benchmarks . Tables: nested headers, merged cells as colspan / rowspan , irregular grids and long financial tables. Charts: every chart becomes an HTML table of its data points, with each value under the right series and label
(82.5 on ParseBench 1 charts, against 69.1 for the next-best open-weight model). Formatting and math: bold, italic, strikethrough , <u>underline</u> , <mark> highlights, <sub> / <sup> , [ ] / [x] checkboxes, [___] blank fields, and formulas in LaTeX, including handwritten ones. Page structure: headers, footers, page numbers and watermarks in their own tags, multi-column text unrolled,
diagrams as Mermaid. One call per page: the text comes from the page image alone, with no layout detector, OCR engine or text layer. Layout boxes are added afterwards. This repository holds the unoptimized BF16 weights . The OCRia-1 that serves LlamaParse is the same model, quantized and served with a speculative decoder and
custom kernels, which makes it about ten times faster. See Speed and The Inference Stack Behind OCRia . OCRia-1 runs inside LlamaParse , which also handles multi-page documents. Examples Pages from ParseBench, rendered at 150 DPI and transcribed with greedy decoding. The right-hand image renders what the
model wrote, without editing. Page OCRia-1 output Dense financial table: a Texas insurance rate filing with a three-level header; the header spans become colspan and the section rows stay in place. Chart as data: a line chart with three series over five years becomes a table of its 15 data points, matching the printed labels. Formatting: a hearing notice with struck-through withdrawn cases, underlined case names and bold times; all three are kept. Handwritten formulas: a handwritten note in Czech; the text is transcribed and each formula written as LaTeX. More examples, including cash-flow statements, bank statements, timetables and economic charts, are in the blog post . Quickstart To run OCRia-1 on your own machine with llama.cpp or Ollama (Linux, Windows, macOS), use the GGUF builds in llamaindex/OCRia-1-GGUF ; the Q8_0 build scores the same as these
weights on a ParseBench 2 sample. On a GPU server: Serve with vLLM 0.30 or later. vLLM compiles kernels for this architecture at start-up and needs the CUDA toolkit
( nvcc ); the vllm/vllm-openai Docker image has it. vllm serve llamaindex/OCRia-1 --served-model-name ocria-1 --max-model-len 32768 \
  --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"image": 1}' Send each page as one image, with prompt.txt as the system message, no user text, and thinking off .
The Qwen3.5 chat template turns thinking on by default, and with it on the model answers in the wrong format. import base64 from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download from openai import OpenAI

prompt = open (hf_hub_download( "llamaindex/OCRia-1" , "prompt.txt" )).read()
page = base64.b64encode( open ( "page.png" , "rb" ).read()).decode()

client = OpenAI(base_url= "http://localhost:8000/v1" , api_key= "EMPTY" )
resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model= "ocria-1" ,
    messages=[
        { "role" : "system" , "content" : prompt},
        { "role" : "user" , "content" : [{ "type" : "image_url" , "image_url" : { "url" : f"data:image/png;base64, {page} " }}]},
    ],
    temperature= 0.0 ,
    max_tokens= 24576 ,
    extra_body={ "chat_template_kwargs" : { "enable_thinking" : False }},
) print (resp.choices[ 0 ].message.content) Offline with vLLM from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams

llm = LLM( "llamaindex/OCRia-1" , max_model_len= 32768 , limit_mm_per_prompt={ "image" : 1 })
messages = [
    { "role" : "system" , "content" : prompt},
    { "role" : "user" , "content" : [{ "type" : "image_url" , "image_url" : { "url" : f"data:image/png;base64, {page} " }}]},
]
out = llm.chat(messages, SamplingParams(temperature= 0.0 , max_tokens= 24576 ),
               chat_template_kwargs={ "enable_thinking" : False }) print (out[ 0 ].outputs[ 0 ].text) With Hugging Face Transformers import torch from PIL import Image from transformers import AutoModelForImageTextToText, AutoProcessor

model = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_pretrained( "llamaindex/OCRia

Neuralink just won the FDA’s approval for a late-stage trial, moving Elon Musk’s brain chip one step closer to market. But the hard part starts now — just ask rival Synchron, which hit pause on its own implant study this month. The details: The LINK trial will assess whether Neuralink’s N1 brain implant can safely and reliably translate neural signals into digital commands. Neuralink says 30+ people have received implants across early trials, logging thousands of hours controlling computers, playing games, and communicating. Recruitment is open, but Neuralink’s hardware remains investigational, with no authorization for general medical use. Why it matters: For people losing movement or speech, brain implants could restore something vital: agency. But Neuralink still has to prove its implant stays safe and reliable for years — rival Synchron paused trials of its own second-gen device this month after a signal-carrying cable underperformed. AMAZON 🪧 Amazon faces strikes in 20+ countries Image source: UNI Global Union The Rundown: Two weeks after an arbitrator handed Amazon its first union contract in North America, unions in 20+ countries are hitting the company with strikes and protests , timed to the Black Friday weekend. The details: UNI Global Union and Progressive International are running the campaign — Make Amazon Pay, now in year seven — with actions scheduled Nov. 27–30. Germany’s Verdi called strikes at 11 Amazon sites, saying pay often doesn’t cover living costs and that the company digitally tracks about 40K employees. The Teamsters are organizing Cyber Monday demonstrations in Los Angeles and Chicago, demanding safer workplaces, better pay, and union recognition. About 800 Amazon workers in British Columbia won Amazon’s first union contract in North America through arbitration, securing raises to C$29 (~$20) an hour and better benefits. A first union contract in Canada and actions in 20+ countries will test whether organized labor can gain real leverage over the company. The details: Parents of 13- to 17-year-olds can set daily screen-time limits, approve new followers, filter keywords, and restrict sensitive content. Nothing switches on until the teen accepts the invite, and an activity log shows the teen every change a parent makes. Searches, viewing history, and posts stay off-limits to parents, with a cap of five teens per parent and one parent per teen. The long-overdue rollout comes amid growing regulatory scrutiny of social media’s impact on minors and controversy surrounding X’s Grok AI chatbot. items.title: Blender, Unreal Engine, Unity, Godot, Roblox with Local Models | Unsloth Documentation
items.content: You can now drive Blender , Unity , Unreal Engine , Godot , Figma and Roblox Studio from Unsloth with local models. In this guide, Unreal Engine, Godot and Blender are all driven by Qwen3.8-27B or Qwen3.8-Flash-Next Unsloth quants: App What you install Port Blender 5.1+ Official Blender MCP add-on 9876 Unity 2021.3+ MCP for Unity package 8080 Unreal Engine 5.8+ Epic's built-in Unreal MCP plugin 8000 Godot 4 Godot MCP Native plugin 9080 Figma (Windows, macOS) Nothing: the desktop app has an MCP server 3845 Roblox Studio (Windows, macOS) Nothing: Studio has an MCP server none Keep the app open on the same computer as Unsloth. In the chat's MCP menu pick it, tick the permission box, then Test connection and Enable . Godot, Figma and Roblox Studio are under More . Not installed means Unsloth did not find the app: see its install step below. Use a model that is good at tool calling, such as Qwen3.8-27B ( UD-Q4_K_XL ). These tools run code in your app, so only the owner account can use them, and they turn off while Remote access or LAN access is on. Other port? Change it under Advanced settings . Other apps: use Add custom MCP or Import config . Blender 1 Install Blender 5.1+ Get it from blender.org . On Linux, extract the .tar.xz with tar and run ./blender . If blender is not on your PATH, set Blender executable under Advanced settings in Unsloth. 2 Install the add-on Turn on Online Access in Edit → Preferences → System . Drag the install button from the Blender MCP add-on page into Blender twice: once for the Blender Lab repository, once for the add-on. 3 Start its bridge The bridge starts with Blender on port 9876 ( Auto Start ). If it is off, open Edit → Preferences → Add-ons → MCP and click Start MCP Bridge Server . Look for Server is running . 4 Connect Unsloth Pick Blender in the MCP menu, tick the permission box, then Test connection and Enable . The first time, Unsloth downloads Blender's MCP server. No display? Run xvfb-run -a ./blender . The bridge does not start with blender -b . Blender example Try: "Use the Blender tools to build a small low-poly island with a sea, a grassy hill, a few trees, a wooden cabin and a warm sun." 7 tool calls, then a render of the result. Unity 1 Install Unity 2021.3+ Install Unity Hub ( Linux steps ), then add an editor under Installs → Install Editor . Also install uv : MCP for Unity runs its server with it. 2 Install MCP for Unity In Window → Package Manager , click + → Add package from git URL and paste https://github.com/CoplayDev/unity-mcp.git?path=/MCPForUnity#main . 3 Start its server Open Window → MCP for Unity , keep the transport on HTTP (port 8080) and start the server. 4 Connect Unsloth Pick Unity in the MCP menu, tick the permission box, then Test connection and Enable . Amber MCP only : the server is up but no Unity Editor has joined yet. Green Connected : ready. Unity example Try: " Use Unity MCP to create a professional-quality low-poly palm prefab with a slender curved trunk and an uneven crown of arching fronds, lime above deep green. Frame the whole tree on warm sand against blue sky with soft side lighting. Check its silhouette at thumbnail size, refine if needed, save the prefab, and show the Game view in chat. " Now that we have our asset, we can also ask Qwen3.8-27B to add it to an existing scene. Keep building in the same chat Once you have a first version, ask for one visible change at a time. For example: “Group the palms toward one side of the island and leave an open stretch of beach. Show me the Game view.” Then use the screenshot to decide what to change next. For longer builds, open Run settings → Tools → Max Tool Calls Per Message and raise the limit, or drag it to Max . If a response stops partway through, try: “Check what’s already in the scene and continue from there.” Edit an existing scene Open a scene you already have and describe what you want to change. Prompt: “Turn this dinosaur beach into a hazy sunset and add three pale turquoise eggs on the sand between the dinosaurs. Keep the camera in place so I can compare the two shots.” Unreal Engine 1 Get Unreal Engine 5.8+ Windows and macOS: the Epic Games Launcher. Linux: the Installed Build , or build from source after linking GitHub in your Epic account ( Connections → Accounts ) and accepting the @EpicGames invite: 2 Turn on the plugin In Edit → Plugins , turn on Unreal MCP and All Toolsets (both off by default), then restart the editor. 3 Start Unreal MCP server The server is off by default. In Edit → Editor Preferences → General → Model Context Protocol , turn on Auto Start Server and restart the editor. It listens on port 8000. 4 Connect Unsloth Pick Unreal Engine in the MCP menu, tick the permission box, then Test connection and Enable . Using the community EngineWire plugin? Set port 3000 and your project folder under Advanced settings . No display? Run Engine/Binaries/Linux/UnrealEditor MyProject.uproject -RenderOffscreen -ModelContextProtocolStartServer . Unsloth is the first desktop app to run and train models. Features • Quickstart • Notebooks • Documentation ⚡ Get started Download the native Unsloth Desktop app for your operating system: Platform Link Windows (x64 and ARM64) Download macOS Download Linux / Ubuntu (deb) Download Linux / Ubuntu (ARM64) (deb) Download Linux (AppImage) Download Download from Unsloth or GitHub Releases . Read guide. Homebrew: brew install --cask unsloth Winget (Windows): winget install -- id UnslothAI.Unsloth - e If endpoint protection blocks irm ... | iex on a managed PC, use winget. Community: Discord 𝕏 (Twitter) Reddit ⭐ Features Unsloth works on Windows, Linux, WSL and macOS . We support Multi GPU setups, NVIDIA, AMD, Intel GPUs, CPUs and the Vulkan backend. Run & Build with AI Run and train LLMs, MLX, GGUF, diffusion, decision, embedding, audio models: Qwen3.8 , GLM-5.3-Flash , Kimi K3 , Qwen-Image-2.1 , MiniMax-H3, DeepSeek-V4 , Gemma 4 . Agents & Tools: Use local models with Claude Code , Codex , and MCP , including tool calling and code execution. Browser & Computer use: Have local LLMs edit your desktop , Edit files & sites , fill out forms, read PDFs Sandboxing: Limit file access for commands your model runs. Search & RAG: Use private and unlimited web search, deep research, auto-compaction (rolling context window) and RAG. Image and video: Run and train image and video diffusion or multimodal models Remote & LAN: Access your local models from any device on LAN or remotely through secure Cloudflare HTTPS. API: Serve models through an OpenAI compatible API . Connect your ChatGPT/Codex subscription, Claude and cloud providers Train & Deploy Fine-tuning: Train LLMs, diffusion, decision, TTS, and embedding models 2× faster with 70% less VRAM with no accuracy loss Complete support: Supports reinforcement learning , LoRA, QLoRA, full fine tuning, pretraining, RL, GRPO, DPO, and FP8. Export & Deploy: Export or Deploy models including GGUF , NVFP4, FP8 and more formats. Datasets: Build datasets from PDFs, CSVs, DOCX files, and more with Data Recipes . 🚀 Unsloth Start Unsloth Start connects Claude Code , Codex and other agents to local models with one command. unsloth start claude --model unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF:UD-Q4_K_XL Agent Command Claude Code unsloth start claude OpenAI Codex unsloth start codex Visual Studio Code unsloth start vscode DeepSeek Harness unsloth start dsh OpenCode unsloth start opencode Hermes Agent unsloth start hermes Pi unsloth start pi OpenClaw unsloth start openclaw Mistral Vibe unsloth start vibe 📥 Install Unsloth can be used in three ways: Unsloth Desktop , the desktop app; Unsloth Studio , the web UI; or Unsloth Core , the code based version. Choose 1024–65515 . If the port is busy, Desktop tries the next 20. It rejects ranges with browser-restricted ports. This covers backend restarts after updates. unsloth studio -p and LAN use separate ports. items.title: Inside the AI Training Data Market — Gabe Greenberg, G2i
items.content:
A frontier lab can pay more for training data it gets to keep exclusive, or take a discount on data another lab can buy too. At AI Engineer CODE, G2i founder Gabe Greenberg tells swyx how labs make that decision, how small pilot orders turn into bigger engagements, and when it makes sense to build a data operation in-house.    We also get into what the labs are buying. A good training task should sit just ahead of what a model can do today. Gabe explains how senior engineers design the task, choose the starting data, and build a verifier that can score the result. items.content:
OCRia-nano-1 Technical report · Blog post · Docs · LiteParse · OCRia-1 · ParseBench OCRia-nano-1 is an 8.1M-parameter model pipeline for document parsing on CPU from LlamaIndex .
It pairs a detector–recognizer OCR stack with LayoutNet, a joint table and layout model, and it runs inside LiteParse , the open-source local document parser. Its models are distilled
from OCRia-1 , our 4B document VLM, with 1/500th of its parameters. Accuracy: 59.2 on ParseBench-2 , ahead of the CPU parsers Indra (55.1) and
Marker (52.5). It lifts LiteParse from 48.7 with Tesseract. See Benchmarks . Speed: 27.8 pages per second on 16 vCPUs, 426 ms per page on one core, twice as fast as LiteParse with Tesseract. Tables and layout: LayoutNet finds tables (rows, columns, spanning header cells) and classifies layout blocks
(headings, lists, captions, page headers and footers) on scanned and born-digital pages. Scripts: a router sends each text line to one of four recognizers: Latin, CJK, right-to-left (Arabic, Hebrew),
and a world-script model for about 17 more scripts. CPU runtime, everywhere LiteParse runs: the CLI, Python and Node.js on Linux, macOS and Windows, and the browser and
edge runtimes through WebAssembly. These are the model files LiteParse runs; they are not a standalone model with its own inference script. LiteParse
renders the page, runs the detector, router and recognizers, merges the OCR text with the PDF text layer, runs
LayoutNet, and writes Markdown or JSON with bounding boxes. Use them through LiteParse (see Quickstart ). Examples Text lines detected on scanned pages, colored by the recognizer the router picked for each line: LayoutNet's layout blocks on two multi-column pages, from the PDF text layer alone: Quickstart Install LiteParse ( pip install liteparse , npm i -g @llamaindex/liteparse or cargo install liteparse ), then pull
the models once. lit models pull downloads this repository's files and ONNX Runtime and checks every file against
its pinned sha256; after that, OCRia-nano-1 is LiteParse's OCR backend by default. lit models pull ocria-nano # once: models + ONNX Runtime (60-75 MB) lit parse scan.pdf --format markdown # OCR, tables and layout with OCRia-nano-1 lit parse scan.pdf --ocr-backend tesseract # force Tesseract for one run Python from liteparse import LiteParse, models

models.pull( "ocria-nano" )
result = LiteParse(ocr_backend= "ocria-nano" , output_format= "markdown" ).parse( "scan.pdf" ) print (result.text) Node.js import { LiteParse , models } from "@llamaindex/liteparse" ;

models. pull ( "ocria-nano" ); const result = await new LiteParse ({ ocrBackend : "ocria-nano" , outputFormat : "markdown" }). parse ( "scan.pdf" ); console . log (result. text ); Browser and edge (WebAssembly) WASM and edge runtimes fully support OCRia-nano. You can also control which models download to minimize download sizes. import init, { LiteParse , OcriaNano } from "@llamaindex/liteparse-wasm" ; await init (); const ocria = await OcriaNano . fromUrl (); // or { scripts: ["latin"], layout: false } for 1.5 MB of models const parser = LiteParse . withOcriaNano ({ ocrEnabled : true , outputFormat : "markdown" }, ocria); const result = await parser. parse (pdfBytes); Input PDFs, images and Office documents (through LiteParse's conversion) Pages render at 250 DPI for OCR by default ( --dpi changes it). Language detection is automatic, the router in OCRia-nano picks a recognizer per line. Output LiteParse's Markdown, text or JSON. With OCRia-nano-1: Content How it is written Tables Markdown tables, or HTML with colspan / rowspan for spanning cells Headings and lists Markdown headings and list items, from LayoutNet's layout classes Page headers and footers removed from the Markdown by default, kept with --keep-headers-footers Layout blocks with --extract-blocks , JSON blocks (heading, paragraph, table, figure, ...) with boxes and links to their text items Words and lines JSON text items with bounding boxes and OCR confidence How it works Model File Role Parameters Line detector det.onnx segmentation map of text lines, depthwise-separable 0.08M Script router router.onnx picks a recognizer per line crop, and detects upside-down lines 0.04M Latin recognizer rec_latin.onnx CTC, int8, supports 791 characters 0.80M World-script recognizer rec_world.onnx CTC, about 17 scripts 0.98M RTL recognizer rec_rtl.onnx CTC, Arabic and Hebrew 0.71M CJK recognizer rec_cjk.onnx CTC, Chinese, Japanese and Korean 1.27M LayoutNet tablenet.bin / tablenet.onnx 6-layer transformer over text units with a CNN image branch: table, row, column, cell and layout-block relations, 13 layout classes 4.27M Total 8.1M The OCR stack is 3.9M parameters. LiteParse runs the ONNX models on ONNX Runtime natively and on tract in WebAssembly. Benchmarks Results from the technical report . Every local system runs on
the same 16-vCPU machine and throughput is measured on 300 random ParseBench pages, with one worker per core. System (CPU) ParseBench-2 OmniParseBench

items.content:
LiteParse | | | | | | Docs English | 简体中文 LiteParse is a standalone OSS PDF parsing tool focused exclusively on fast and light parsing. It provides high-quality spatial text parsing with bounding boxes, without proprietary LLM features or cloud dependencies. Everything runs locally on your machine. Hitting the limits of local parsing? For complex documents (dense tables, multi-column layouts, charts, handwritten text, or
scanned PDFs), you'll get significantly better results with LlamaParse ,
our cloud-based document parser built for production document pipelines. LlamaParse handles the
hard stuff so your models see clean, structured data and markdown. Sign up for LlamaParse free Overview Fast Text Parsing : Spatial text parsing using PDFium, ~2-5ms per page Flexible OCR System : Built-in : Tesseract (zero setup, bundled with the library) OCRia-nano-1 (opt-in) : LiteParse's own CPU models (8.1M parameters): line detector, script router, four recognizers and LayoutNet, a learned table and layout model. lit models pull ocria-nano once, then it is the OCR backend ( details ) HTTP Servers : Plug in any OCR server (EasyOCR, PaddleOCR, custom) Standard API : Simple, well-defined OCR API specification Complexity Detection : Cheaply check whether a document needs OCR or heavier parsing — route, reject, or estimate cost before a full parse Screenshot Generation : Generate high-quality page screenshots for LLM agents Multiple Output Formats : Markdown, JSON, and Text Markdown Output : Structured Markdown with headings, tables, lists, images, and links — great for feeding LLMs and RAG pipelines Bounding Boxes : Precise text positioning information Multi-language : Use from Rust, Node.js/TypeScript, Python, or the browser (WASM) Worker Pool Mode (Python & Node.js): Parse in persistent worker processes for true parallelism (PDFium otherwise serializes concurrent parses) and hard per-parse timeouts — rogue documents are killed, identified by name, and never stall the pipeline Multi-platform : Linux, macOS (Intel/ARM), Windows flowchart LR

our cloud-based document parser built for production document pipelines. LlamaParse handles the

hard stuff so your models see clean, structured data and markdown. items.title: Trump is destroying the rule of law in the US – to protect himself and the tech titans he worships as new gods | Jonathan Freedland
items.content: To get Jensen Huang back at Nvidia, the president trampled on the justice system, national security and the trust America needs to do business in the global economyDon’t let the sex distract you. Or the lies or the boardroom intrigue or even the AI-generated bra, all of which could have come from an especially wild episode of Succession. Don’t let that lure you into thinking that the Jensen Huang affair is, as Donald Trump would have it, little more than a sex scandal involving a corporate maestro. It is much more serious than that. The events of the past week tell instead a story of legal immunity and indeed impunity – revealing how Trump is putting himself, the tech bros and even artificial intelligence above the law.It can be hard to see that through the thicket of questions that surround this episode, each one of which, don’t get me wrong, merits attention. Consider the personal profit Trump made thanks to his re-installation of Huang as the CEO of Nvidia, the world’s leading maker of advanced AI chips. Breaking the norm observed by previous presidents who, keen to avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest, either divested themselves of stock holdings or placed them in a blind trust, Trump cheerfully buys and sells stocks in companies whose fates he can influence. He saw the value of his shares in Nvidia plunge when Huang was forced out, following revelations that the CEO had had an affair with Alice Huang, reportedly an asset of Chinese intelligence. Last weekend Trump urged the board to reconsider; Huang was reinstated on Monday and Nvidia’s value promptly soared – putting $15m in Trump’s pocket. Not for the first time, he had used the power of his office to enrich himself.Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? items.title: How Recent AI Model Advances Are Reshaping Tech Jobs | Urban Institute
items.content: Summer releases and strategic pivots Publicly available AI models made qualitative leaps in capabilities this summer. Anthropic launched Claude Fable 5 on June 9, suspended access on June 12 following a US export-control directive citing national security, and restored general access on July 1 . In early September, OpenAI released GPT-5.6 Sol and then GPT-6 Astra, both on par with Fable in many capabilities. Other labs’ proprietary and open-weight models generally trail GPT and Claude. Over the past year, AI labs have focused increasingly on software design and implementation, driven by pressure to monetize. Building and serving frontier models costs hundreds of billions of dollars. Anthropic and OpenAI both confidentially filed for initial public offerings in early June. Coding, among AI’s most lucrative applications, is where they have concentrated their efforts. AI-driven software development, once met with deep skepticism, is now the norm. Engineers now set goals and constraints for AI agents instead of writing and debugging code by hand. This hits junior roles hardest. Their core tasks (debugging, small patches, routine implementation, and testing) are now done by AI. Software, a lucrative market for AI, is the first field where AI does much of the work. The tasks it absorbed once trained new engineers; without new on-ramps that teach directing and checking AI, the senior pipeline will thin, an early warning for other white-collar jobs. Breakthroughs in mathematics and engineering The most dramatic recent development has been in pure mathematics. This year, AI models began solving open problems that had stymied mathematicians for decades. In September, OpenAI published a proposed solution to the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize problem, accompanied by a proof formalized in Lean. The Clay Mathematics Institute subsequently said the problem appeared to have been settled, while emphasizing its evaluation process. OpenAI released more than 700 mathematical manuscripts, with results at different stages of verification. The field is being rapidly upended, and how mathematicians adapt may show how other professions will adjust as AI overtakes their work. This matters for most technical fields, because mathematical modeling underpins all science and technology. Widespread access to fast, reliable AI modeling will likely drive sweeping scientific and technological advances. The biggest immediate impact may again be on software development, which remains largely trial and error. The methods that solve math problems can also prove that code will work or generate it from a description of what it must do. Formal verification can establish specified properties, while specification checks and integration testing remain necessary . AI’s math breakthroughs show that more education no longer guarantees protection from automation . Research may accelerate, but technical work will shift toward framing problems and judging AI’s answers, and verified code could shrink testing jobs, a key entry point. STEM education must adapt. Physical-world reasoning, biotech, and cybersecurity AI also made a major leap in modeling the physical 3D world. OpenAI reports that Astra achieves 95.9 percent geometric overlap on BenchCAD , which tests reconstruction of objects from images by generating CAD code, compared with 83.3 percent for GPT‑5.6 Sol. Online demos showed Astra, guided by a few reference images and simple prompts, recreating landmarks and building working mechanical contraptions. 3D reasoning is also aiding biotechnology. In August, Claude Mythos Preview and Opus 4.8, operating specialist design tools, produced binders for 14 of 15 evaluable targets, with 22–35 percent of designs binding depending on the setup. In cybersecurity, AI is speeding up both the discovery and repair of software flaws and their exploitation. On October 6, Anthropic reported that its Glasswing partners had used Claude to find at least 129,000 verified vulnerabilities based on partial partner reporting between April and July. Fixing flaws quickly matters more as software spreads into cars, robots, and lab equipment. But the same skills that detect threats can power attacks, and while the most capable models remain with top labs and their partners, open “unaligned” models are advancing. As AI moves into the physical world, drafting, 3D design, and lab research come into scope, with work shifting toward real-world testing of AI’s designs . In cybersecurity, workers who can triage and quickly fix AI-found flaws grow more valuable as attackers gain similar tools. AI is not only a white-collar issue. Looking ahead The final quarter is typically busy for major AI releases, so more-advanced models are likely coming soon. This summer’s advances share one thread: a shift from humans doing the work to humans directing AI and checking its output. Workers with the support and ability to adapt will be best positioned for what comes next. The most valuable skills will

items.title: nexos.ai AI Adoption Platform puts 200+ models behind one AI Gateway, with budget limits and governance built in
items.content:
nexos.ai is an all-in-one AI platform for enterprise AI adoption. It brings full control and governance to every team. The AI gateway at its core routes every LLM request through one unified layer where budgets, policies, and audit trails apply. 



Here’s how it governs usage, optimizes AI spend, and meets the compliance requirements EU companies set.



TL;DR




Governance. Adopt AI with control. Set who can use which models, apply budgets and usage limits, and manage permissions from one place.



Compliance. SOC 2 Type 2, ISO 27001, and ISO 42001 certified, and fully GDPR compliant.



Cost control. Smart Router and LLM caching allow AI spend optimization. Cost tracking attributes every dollar to a team, project, or user.



European hosting. The platform and most available models are hosted in Europe, with zero data retention and no training on your data.



Visibility. LLM observability shows usage, cost, and routing decisions across every team.




Why does AI adoption need a control layer?



Teams often start using AI on their own. Marketing picks one tool, engineering picks another, and each team signs up for its own API keys. Spend grows faster than anyone’s view of it, and leadership sees the total on the monthly invoice.



The EU AI Act adds a second pressure. It moves AI governance and accountability from policy documents into daily operations. CTOs and CISOs now need shared answers on which models are used, what data goes into them, and what each team spends.



What does the nexos.ai AI gateway do?



An AI gateway sits between your applications and the model providers they call. Developers keep one API and their existing SDKs. Leadership gets one place to set and enforce rules. The nexos.ai AI gateway handles three jobs.




Governance and control. Admins set which models each team can access and enforce policies centrally.



Spend optimization. Requests are routed, cached, and compressed so routine work uses cheaper models and fewer tokens.



Reliability. When a provider goes down or slows, automatic fallbacks reroute requests to another model or provider.




The same endpoint reaches 200+ leading AI models, so teams can adopt new models without locking into one vendor.



How does the gateway govern AI usage?



Admins decide which teams and users can reach which models. They set budgets and usage limits per team or user. Policy enforcement applies those rules to every request, and audit logs and traces record each one.



Usage is visible by team and project. When finance or an auditor asks who used what, the answer is in the logs.



The gateway works alongside Chat & Agents. Employees adopt AI in daily work there, chatting with leading AI models and building no-code agents under the same permissions, budgets, and audit trails.



How does it optimize AI spend?



The gateway reduces spend in four ways. None of them require changes to your applications.




Smart Router. Each request goes to a model chosen on cost, quality, and latency. Routine workloads stop using premium models.



LLM caching. Identical requests aren’t paid for twice. Caching lowers both latency and token spend.



Context compression. The gateway sends fewer tokens to the model, which lowers cost before the request reaches the LLM.



Cost tracking and controls. Spend is tracked in real time and attributed to a team, project, or user, down to the request.




Teams see where money goes before the invoice arrives. They can also measure the savings from routing, caching, and request optimization as they happen.



What compliance and security does it cover?



This list covers what nexos.ai provides for security and compliance reviews.




Certifications. nexos.ai is SOC 2 Type 2, ISO 27001, and ISO 42001 certified.



Regulation. The platform is fully GDPR compliant.



Hosting. The platform and most available models are hosted in Europe.



Data handling. Zero data retention is available for supported models, and your data isn’t used to train AI models unless you allow it.



Access. SSO and RBAC protect sensitive information.




Certifications, European hosting, and zero data retention give security and compliance teams a clear basis for approval. Teams can still pick the LLM that fits their own preferences and compliance requirements.



What do teams and leadership each get?



The AI gateway serves two groups at once. Teams get tools to build with, and leadership gets the controls to scale AI adoption safely.



Teams get one API for every leading LLM, access to 200+ models, production-ready infrastructure, and no vendor lock-in.



Leadership gets visibility into AI usage and costs, one invoice with budget and spend controls, policy enforcement, and audit logs and traces.



How do you get started with nexos.ai?

items.title: Architectural Patterns for Deterministic AI Pipelines
items.content:
When you’re handing over too much control to LLMs, there’s a risk of getting flooded with output that’s hard to audit, with a low chance of producing the same results ever again. This structure also has unpredictable costs, and depending on a model’s reaction, one run could include multiple costly tool calls.Implementing intentional deterministic components provides known cost ceilings and accurate, repeatable outcomes. Deterministic AI pipelines are a spectrum, and you choose the balance.Deterministic AI vs. non-deterministic AI: What are your options?Deterministic AI are systems that provide predictable output. They give the same (or very similar) result for the same input, making them fully auditable, transparent, and safe to use in regulated environments. You can expect direct output with little to no randomness and hallucination risk, which is usually associated with LLMs.Deterministic systems are more rigid, but at the same time they provide predictable outputs. Non-deterministic systems work exactly opposite.On the other hand, non-deterministic AI relies on probabilistic responses. You’re unlikely to get the same response even if you use exactly the same prompt in the same LLM. You’ll experience run-to-run variations and adjustable randomness.These paths aren’t mutually exclusive, and a hybrid approach can be a successful strategy. Here’s a quick overview:Fully deterministic: The input always produces the same output.Agentic workflow: A structure that pairs deterministic control with probabilistic AI reasoning.Fully autonomous agent: An AI system capable of autonomously examining its environment, breaking a goal into tasks, and executing steps.Teams may balance speed, cost, and security with a blend of non-deterministic and deterministic AI, meaning they mindfully decide where models run to maintain governance and token use.Why production AI pipelines need deterministic componentsBuilding a production pipeline requires a reliable end-to-end process, and by using AI, there’s the possibility of deviations and hallucinations. When you add deterministic components to the mix, you’re left with a trustworthy production cycle that only needs human intervention in sensitive cases.Here are a few reasons to include deterministic elements in your pipeline:Reliable outcomes: Knowing outcomes are predictable allows teams to implement production pipelines at scale, even in heavily regulated industries. Easy testing and debugging: Deterministic processes include gates and guardrails, which reveal points of failure quickly, allowing for simpler testing and debugging. Predictable costs: Fixed steps have flat costs, and controlling where the model runs provides a firm cost ceiling.How do the core architectural patterns for deterministic AI pipelines work? You might hesitate when deploying an agent for production, as you’re facing the possibility of an untenable error loop, and each retry or tool call adds tokens. A strong architectural pattern creates a workflow that holds up in production. A typical pattern should include: In practice, non-deterministic actions from the AI Agent are placed inside a deterministic shell, so that input and output steps always work as intended.The deterministic shell: When you’re deploying an LLM or agent, you want to know that the actions are contained within certain rules. The deterministic shell provides a rule-based system of what’s allowed and what isn’t, along with what should happen in both those events. The input layer: This layer is also known as the context engineering layer or deterministic orchestration layer, and it provides the blueprint for the workflow states and sequences. Some teams may use caching to return the same output for the same input.Validation or test: A rule-based component that tests the output to ensure it meets the requirements before you execute. It flags non-compliance and prompts you for the next step.Human oversight: Despite the accuracy of deterministic AI, human oversight still provides necessary judgment that AI models can’t safely replicate, especially with sensitive actions. Mixing deterministic and non-deterministic components is a deliberate architectural decision. When you follow a pipeline relying on a pure agentic workflow, you may run into unpredictable routing and untestable business logic. To build a strong, scalable pipeline, teams need to decide where the model decides and where it doesn’t.How n8n handles deterministic logic in AI workflowsn8n is an AI-native, source-available workflow automation platform that lets you build a hybrid agentic workflow on a visual canvas. Here’s how n8n lets you build a reliable production pipeline.Deterministic shell routingIF and Switch nodes route outputs inside one workflow. These nodes rely on precise conditions. The If node relies on yes/no or true/false determinations, so the workflow can only follow certain paths. The If node works well for binary decisions, and you can use it to combine multiple rules, including and/or logic. The Switch node is similar to the If node, but it supports multiple output routes. Switch is suitable for data handling that requires different levels of effort or has varying priority levels. Validation The Code node lets you use JavaScript or Python for complex data manipulation when you need advanced logic. When you’re running deterministic AI workflows, the Code node is helpful for data validation and transformation. You might apply your own rules to a workflow, like checking that values fall within allowed ranges.n8n also includes the Structured Output Parser, a sub-node that allows you to require a specific output format. Provide a JSON schema or example, and the parser enforces a specific format.Purposeful agent useYou can place n8n’s AI Agent node directly in a visual workflow, giving you a reasoning layer you can place precisely where you need it. Attach specific tools, and determine the inputs and intent before the agent chooses the correct next step to follow. 💡With the new n8n Agents feature, users can create AI Agents from the simplified UI. Once created and tested manually, such agents can be called from the workflow, too. Human oversightImplement human-in-the-loop steps where workflows call for human judgment. Teams can require approval on tool calls, so the workflow pauses and waits for a person to approve or deny the action. This is optional per tool, not a universal stop.💡There’s a related process called human-on-the-loop, where humans review results and handle exceptions. Both structures are useful depending on the level of oversight you need.Execution history and cachingExecution history provides an audit layer that lets you review runs, each one showing steps taken and the result. On self-hosted plans, you can trace executions with OpenTelemetry, allowing you to monitor execution latency, track requests, view token use, and debug failures. n8n helps encourage AI governance through deterministic caching. Before the AI model runs, the workflow can check the input in a Data Table. An If node can look for a match: On a hit, the workflow returns the stored results, and on a miss, the model runs, and the result is added to the store.



Achieve reliable outputs with n8nProbabilistic outcomes don’t work for every scenario. Deterministic AI provides a safety net for when you can’t afford to make mistakes, whether you’re facing strict compliance rulings or expensive token use. n8n lets you take a hybrid approach. Use deterministic steps where it’s more secure and cost predictable, and use non-deterministic AI where you need advanced reasoning. The n8n Production AI Playbook walks you through the steps to create workflows that match your needs. Ready to design production-ready pipelines?
